blocks.text: In **whole report**, the person sees a flashed array of letters and names as many as they can. In **Sperling's (1960)** display that was **12 letters in three rows of four**, and people averaged only about **4.5 of 12 letters** (about **37.5%**). **Partial report** works differently: a **tone played after the display disappears** tells the person which one row to name.
children: Whole report asks for everything, and partial report asks for one cued row.

blocks.text: Because people cannot know in advance which row will be cued, they cannot memorize just one. Yet they averaged about **3.3 of 4 letters** (about **82%**) **whichever row was cued**. For instance, with rows like X M L T, A F N B and C D Z P, people reported only a few letters when asked for everything but nearly all of whichever row the tone picked out.
children: Success on any cued row means information about all rows was available at the start.

blocks.text: So **the whole-report limit is a limit on how much can be reported before the trace fades, not on how much was perceived**. It would be a mistake to read the 82% as proof that every letter was stored perfectly, since it is accuracy on the cued row. What matters is that the tone came after the display was gone.
children: Whole report measures what survives the reporting, and partial report reveals what was there.

blocks.text: In both conditions the person selects a row after a cue tone. In **immediate partial report** the cue comes right as the display ends, so the trace is still strong and accuracy was about **3.3 of 4 letters** (about **82%**). In **delayed partial report** the cue is held back by an extra delay, and accuracy fell to about **1 of 4 letters** (**25%**).
children: The two conditions differ only in how long the person waits for the cue.

blocks.text: Since waiting is the only thing that changes, the drop shows that the **sensory trace is fading fast**. As the cue is delayed, partial-report accuracy falls toward the **whole-report** level. In **Sperling (1960)**, the same cue that gave about 82% when immediate gave about 25% when it arrived after the delay.
children: Longer delay means lower accuracy, trending toward the whole-report level.

blocks.text: This is why **sensory memory has a large capacity but a very short duration**, with most information lost within about **one second** unless it is selected. The fall does not mean the letters were never seen. It means the representation faded before the cue could be used to select from it.
children: Large capacity does not rescue information from fast decay.

blocks.text: **Sensory memory** and **short-term memory** are two stores of **Atkinson and Shiffrin's (1968)** modal model, and they differ in how much they hold and how long it lasts. Sensory memory briefly retains incoming stimulation for seconds or fractions of a second, with a **very large capacity**. Short-term memory holds about **five to seven items** for roughly **fifteen to twenty seconds**.
children: Sensory memory holds a lot for an instant, and short-term memory holds a little for longer.

blocks.text: **Sperling's (1960)** immediate cue let people report almost any row because so much was still in sensory memory, and a delayed cue arrived after most of it had faded. **Attention** is what moves selected information from the first store into the second. For instance, a phone directory floods sensory memory with many numbers, attention picks out the one you want, and repeating it keeps it in short-term memory long enough to dial.
children: Attention is the gate between the two stores.
Rehearsal keeps the selected item available.

blocks.text: It would be a mistake to describe short-term memory as just a longer sensory memory. Sensory memory is large and fleeting, while short-term memory is small and depends on selection and rehearsal.
children: The two stores differ in kind, not only in duration.

blocks.text: The **icon** is the fleeting **visual** trace left by stimulation, and the **echo** is the brief continuation of **auditory** information after a sound ends. Both are forms of **sensory memory**, so the only real difference is the sense involved: seeing for the icon and hearing for the echo.
children: Icon is visual sensory memory, and echo is auditory sensory memory.

blocks.text: **Persistence of vision**, such as a sparkler seeming to leave a trail, shows the icon at work, and **Sperling (1960)** studied iconic memory with flashed letters. For the echo, think of how you can still replay the last few words someone said for a moment after they stop.
children: Each trace lingers briefly after the stimulus is gone.

blocks.text: Both traces fade within seconds or fractions of a second, and neither is the durable representation used to remember something much later. A large capacity does not mean a long duration.
children: Both are large but short-lived.

blocks.text: **Decay** says a memory trace weakens simply because **time passes**, so it predicts the same loss at the same delay on every trial. **Interference** says other memories compete with the one being tested, so loss depends on **how much competing material there is**, not only on time.
children: Decay depends on time alone, and interference depends on competing material.

blocks.text: In **Brown (1958)** and **Peterson and Peterson (1959)**, participants saw **three letters and a number** and counted backward by threes for **3 to 18 seconds**, which blocks rehearsal. The average over all trials fell steadily, and Peterson and Peterson read that as decay.
children: Backward counting blocks rehearsal, so forgetting could be attributed to time.

blocks.text: But at 18 seconds recall was relatively **high on trial 1**, lower by trial 3, and **very low after many trials**, so the same delay did far more damage when more earlier sets had piled up. That trial-by-trial pattern points to **proactive interference**, which **Keppel and Underwood (1962)** offered as the alternative account. An answer that says forgetting happened because of time but ignores the trial history is describing decay when the pattern shows interference.
children: Same delay, different recall, so time alone cannot explain the loss.

blocks.text: **Retroactive interference** is when **new information disrupts memory for older information**, so the memory that suffers is the old one and the competitor arrived later. **Proactive interference** is when **old information disrupts memory for newer information**, so the memory that suffers is the new one and the competitor arrived earlier.
children: Retroactive harms backward in time, and proactive harms forward in time.

blocks.text: To label a case correctly, first decide **which information the person is trying to recall**, then ask whether the competing information came before or after it. Earlier competing material is proactive and later competing material is retroactive. It would be a mistake to pick by which memory is newer in general, because the question is always the direction of harm relative to the item being recalled.
children: Identify the target first, then check whether the competitor came before or after.

blocks.text: For instance, learning a new phone number and then struggling to recall the old one is retroactive. Previous parking spots making today's spot hard to remember is proactive, and so are earlier trigrams harming recall of the current one in **Brown (1958)** and **Peterson and Peterson (1959)**. Routine events are especially vulnerable because similar memories compete, and both kinds are reduced when events are distinctive.
children: Similar, routine memories compete most, and distinctiveness protects against both kinds.

title: Average over all trials vs trial-by-trial recall

blocks.text: The **average over all trials** pools every trial together, so recall appears to drop steadily as the delay grows from **3 to 18 seconds**, as though short-term memory simply decays. **Trial-by-trial recall** looks at early and late trials separately. Early trials keep **high recall even at 18 seconds**, and later trials show **very low recall at the same delay**.
children: Pooling shows a smooth decline, and separating trials shows a split.

blocks.text: In **Brown (1958)** and **Peterson and Peterson (1959)**, recall at 18 seconds was relatively high on trial one, lower by trial three, and substantially reduced after many trials. The average blends early trials with high recall and late trials with very low recall, so it hides where the steep drop actually comes from.
children: Averaging blends good early trials with poor late trials.

blocks.text: The steep drop in the average comes mostly from the later trials, where **proactive interference** has built up. Averaging therefore hides the interference behind something that looks like decay. This is why the Brown-Peterson pattern is evidence for interference and not only for time-based decay.
children: The apparent decay is largely built-up interference.

blocks.text: **Maintenance rehearsal** is repeating information, such as silently saying a label or number, to prolong how long it stays available in **short-term memory**. It keeps information alive only while the repeating continues. For instance, repeating a label over and over keeps it available.
children: Maintenance keeps information available only as long as you keep repeating it.

blocks.text: **Elaborative rehearsal** is linking new information to **knowledge already in long-term memory**, such as explaining how it relates to what you know. Adding meaning supports learning that lasts longer. Explaining how that same label relates to something you already know is the elaborative version.
children: Elaborative rehearsal works through meaning and connections.

blocks.text: Repetition is not the same as understanding. If the question stresses meaning or links to existing knowledge, the answer is elaborative. **Recoding** is a third control process, which reorganizes or modifies information that is already in short-term memory.
children: Repeat to hold, connect to learn, and recode to reorganize.

title: Miller's seven plus or minus two vs three to four items

blocks.text: **Miller's (1956)** estimate of short-term capacity is **seven plus or minus two units**, where a unit can be a digit, word, number or phrase and differs across tasks. Because units can hold different amounts of information, the title does not prove that every system holds exactly seven raw items.
children: Miller's figure counts units, and units vary in size.

blocks.text: **Alvarez and Cavanagh (2004)** estimated **about three to four items** for visual short-term memory using change detection. The first array stayed up for **100 milliseconds**, the second for **2,000 milliseconds**, and people judged whether the two matched. Accuracy fell sharply above roughly four items, and colored squares gave a higher estimated capacity than complex polygons or shaded cubes.
children: Visual change detection gives a smaller estimate, and it depends on object complexity.

blocks.text: The figures come from different places: **five to seven** is the modal-model estimate for short-term memory, seven plus or minus two is Miller's, and three to four is Alvarez and Cavanagh's for visual objects. Different tasks need not measure one identical capacity, so seven should not be treated as a universal limit for visual memory.
children: Each number belongs to its own source and task.

blocks.text: An **item** is one basic unit, such as a single digit, letter or word. A **chunk** is a larger meaningful unit built from smaller ones, such as a familiar group of digits. **Chunking** lets each slot in short-term memory carry more information, so the same limited number of units holds more.
children: A chunk packs several items into one slot.

blocks.text: For instance, **Ericsson and colleagues (1980)** trained a student to reach a digit span of **79** by treating strings of digits as familiar **running times**, so each running time was one chunk. The gain comes from knowledge-based organization, not from enlarging every raw limit equally.
children: Familiar knowledge makes the chunks.

blocks.text: A big span after training does not mean the memory system itself got bigger. It means each unit holds more.
children: The slots stayed the same size, but each one holds more.

blocks.text: **Episodic memory** is memory for **personal events tied to a particular time and place**, and **Tulving** described it as a kind of mental time travel. **Semantic memory** is memory for **facts and general knowledge** that is not tied to the moment you learned it. Episodic answers 'what happened to me then', and semantic answers 'what do I know'.
children: Episodic is tied to a moment, and semantic is general knowledge.

blocks.text: For instance, remembering one particular birthday party is episodic, and knowing what a birthday is is semantic.
children: The party is an event, and the concept is a fact.

blocks.text: Both are branches of **declarative memory** inside long-term memory, and the other major branch of long-term memory is **procedural memory**, which concerns skills. They are classified by function, not by how long they last. Neither is an extra short-term store, since they sit in long-term memory.
children: Both are long-term declarative memory.

blocks.text: **Duration** is how long information stays available in short-term memory, roughly **fifteen to twenty seconds** without rehearsal. **Capacity** is how much can be held at once, traditionally about **seven plus or minus two units**. A question about how long is duration, and a question about how much is capacity.
children: Duration is time, and capacity is amount.

blocks.text: Each can be changed by a strategy: **rehearsal prolongs duration**, and **chunking raises effective capacity**. Counting backward blocks rehearsal in **Brown (1958)** and **Peterson and Peterson (1959)**, so a trigram is lost within about fifteen to twenty seconds. **Ericsson and colleagues (1980)** raised a digit span to **79** by chunking.
children: Rehearsal affects duration, and chunking affects capacity.

blocks.text: So when a result changes, ask which strategy was used and not only which memory system is involved. Mixing up the two is a common slip.
children: Name the strategy first, then decide which property it changed.

blocks.text: **Short-term memory** in the sense of **Atkinson and Shiffrin (1968)** is a single component that holds what has been selected for a short time. Rehearsal keeps its contents available, and the emphasis is on **temporary availability**. **Working memory (Baddeley and Hitch, 1974)** is a limited-capacity system for the temporary **storage and manipulation** of information.
children: Short-term memory emphasizes holding, and working memory emphasizes holding and working on.

blocks.text: The working-memory model treats memory as active: information is held and worked on at the same time. It has a **central executive**, a **phonological loop** and a **visuospatial sketchpad**, and it separates verbal and auditory information from visual and spatial information. **Baddeley** added the **episodic buffer in 2000**, so it belongs to the expanded model.
children: Working memory has separate components coordinated by the executive.

blocks.text: For instance, in 43 × 6, the 8 from 3 × 6 = 18 is held (storage) while the 1 is carried and 6 × 4 = 24 is computed (an operation). The 8 has to survive while other steps run. It would be a mistake to call working memory passive storage, since comprehension, learning and reasoning need holding and operating together.
children: Storage plus operation together is the mark of working memory.

blocks.text: The **phonological loop** maintains **verbal and auditory** information, with a **phonological store** that holds it and an **articulatory rehearsal** process that repeats the sounds, even silently. The **visuospatial sketchpad** holds **visual** information (what something looks like) and **spatial** information (where its parts are and how they are arranged).
children: The loop handles sounds and words, and the sketchpad handles shapes and locations.

blocks.text: To tell them apart, ask whether the content is sounds and words or shapes and locations. For instance, a remembered sentence uses the loop, and the remembered shape of an F uses the sketchpad. **Brooks's (1968)** opposite results show the two are at least partly independent.
children: Content type decides which system is used.
Brooks's results show the systems are partly independent.

blocks.text: Both interact with long-term knowledge, so one calculation can use verbal rehearsal of a result together with a picture of the digits. The **central executive** is not a store for any particular kind of content. It directs and coordinates the other two.
children: The executive controls the two stores and does not hold content itself.

title: Brooks's sentence task vs F task

blocks.text: In **Brooks's (1968)** **sentence task**, people memorized a sentence and decided for each word whether it was a noun, responding by speaking or by pointing. **Pointing was easier**. In the **F task**, people memorized the shape of an F and classified each corner as inside or outside, responding by speaking or by pointing. **Speaking was easier**.
children: The sentence task favored pointing, and the F task favored speaking.

blocks.text: In the sentence task, holding the sentence used the **phonological loop**, so speaking the answers competed with it. In the F task, following the F used the **sketchpad**, so pointing to spatially arranged responses competed with it.
children: Interference appears when the response uses the same system as the held information.

blocks.text: A task is easier when the information held and the operation performed use **different types of short-term memory**. Memorize the logic and not just the result: the easier response is the one that uses the other system.
children: Hold in one system, respond with the other.

blocks.text: The **phonological store** is the part of the phonological loop that holds verbal and auditory information for a short time. The **articulatory rehearsal process** is the part that keeps the contents active by repeating the sounds, even silently.
children: The store holds the sounds, and rehearsal refreshes them.

blocks.text: **Articulatory suppression**, speaking while trying to memorize, occupies the rehearsal process. For instance, repeating an unrelated word while trying to memorize a list leaves the rehearsal process busy. That reduces recall, and it reduces both the **word-length effect** (because short words no longer win by being quicker to rehearse) and the **phonological similarity effect** (because converting seen items into sounds is disrupted).
children: Suppression blocks rehearsal and removes effects that depend on it.

blocks.text: Suppression does not erase the store. It blocks the process that refreshes it.
children: The store is intact, but it is no longer being refreshed.

title: Word-length effect vs phonological similarity effect

blocks.text: The **word-length effect** is that lists of short words are remembered better than lists of long words, because longer words take more time to say and rehearse. The **phonological similarity effect** is that items that sound alike are confused with each other, even when they look different. For instance, E is confused with B because they sound alike.
children: Word length concerns rehearsal time, and similarity concerns overlapping sound codes.

blocks.text: **Baddeley and colleagues (1975, 1984)** found more short words were recalled than long words. **Ellis and Hennelly (1980)** found Welsh-English bilingual children had a shorter digit span in Welsh because Welsh number names take longer to say. Span tracks how much can be said in about **1.5 to 2 seconds**, so the language difference follows the time to say the number names and not the numbers themselves.
children: Speech time, not the quantity of items, sets the span.

blocks.text: Both effects support the idea that verbal maintenance depends on **sound-based codes** and speech-related rehearsal, and articulatory suppression reduces both.
children: Both effects depend on sound codes in the loop.

title: Central executive vs the two storage systems

blocks.text: The **central executive** is about **control**: it directs and maintains attention, divides attention, switches it when the task changes, suppresses irrelevant information, coordinates the other components and performs calculations. The **phonological loop and sketchpad** are about **content**: verbal and auditory for the loop, visual and spatial for the sketchpad.
children: The executive controls, and the two storage systems hold and rehearse.

blocks.text: For instance, following a phone number while giving directions needs the executive to split attention while the loop rehearses the digits. It would be a mistake to describe the executive as storing information.
children: The executive splits attention and the loop holds the digits.

blocks.text: Naming a controller does not explain how control is done, which is why the executive is criticized as a **homunculus**. It is today often split into **updating, shifting and inhibition** (**Miyake and colleagues, 2000**).
children: Modern accounts break the executive into specific functions.

blocks.text: **Updating** is changing the information currently being maintained as new information arrives. **Shifting** is changing the task or operation being performed. **Miyake and colleagues (2000)** separate these two from **inhibition**, which suppresses information or responses that interfere with the goal.
children: Updating changes contents, shifting changes operations, and inhibition blocks interference.

blocks.text: For instance, replacing the contents you are holding with new ones is updating, switching from adding to multiplying is shifting, and ignoring a distracting number is inhibition. Updating is about the contents of memory, shifting is about the operation, and inhibition is about what to block.
children: Ask whether the change is in contents, in operation, or in what gets blocked.

blocks.text: All three are functions inside what would otherwise be one broad label, the executive.
children: The three functions give the executive specific parts.

title: Original three-part model vs the episodic buffer

blocks.text: The **original model** has three parts proposed by **Baddeley and Hitch (1974)**: the central executive, the phonological loop and the visuospatial sketchpad. The **episodic buffer (Baddeley, 2000)** is a **fourth component** of limited capacity, about **four chunks**, that binds information from the loop, the sketchpad and long-term memory into integrated episodes. The buffer is not part of the original three-component proposal.
children: The buffer is a later fourth component that binds information together.

blocks.text: The buffer is needed because people can immediately recall about **16 words** from a meaningful sentence, more than their span for unrelated words. Meaning and long-term language knowledge let the words stay connected, so a sentence's words are kept together as connected material and not as 16 separate items.
children: Meaning lets many words be held as one connected episode.

blocks.text: Some **amnesic patients** can immediately recall a just-heard story. That suggests immediate retention of an organized episode can survive when longer-term memory is impaired.
children: Immediate episodic retention can be separate from long-term memory.

blocks.text: **Vogel and colleagues (2005)** recorded **event-related potentials** during a task where **red bars** were shown for **100 milliseconds** and held across a **900 millisecond** retention interval. For **high-capacity participants**, adding two blue distractors to two red targets changed the response little, because they kept the irrelevant blue bars out of working memory. For **low-capacity participants**, the same distractors raised the response toward the four-item level, because they let the bars in.
children: High-capacity people filter out distractors, and low-capacity people let them in.

blocks.text: **Capacity was positively correlated with filtering efficiency**, so people with higher capacity are also less distracted. A lower score can reflect competing material occupying processing the targets needed.
children: Capacity depends on what is kept out as well as what is held.

blocks.text: Capacity here is not only about holding items. It is also about keeping the wrong ones out.
children: Good capacity includes good filtering.

title: Rotating a representation vs storing a fixed picture

blocks.text: If a person merely **stored an unchanged picture**, holding the image as it was seen with no operation applied, then deciding whether two views match would take about the same time whatever the angle between them. **Mental rotation** instead turns an internal representation to line it up with the other view, in the picture plane or in depth. A bigger angle needs more turning, so it takes longer.
children: A fixed picture predicts no angle effect, and rotation predicts a longer time for bigger angles.

blocks.text: **Shepard and Metzler (1971)** showed pairs of block-built objects at different orientations and asked whether they matched. For picture-plane pairs, **reaction time rose approximately linearly with the angle**, so small angles were answered faster than large ones.
children: Reaction time increased steadily with the angle between the views.

blocks.text: A static copy would predict no angle effect, so the pattern points to an **active operation on a spatial representation**. The evidence is the shape of the reaction-time curve and not what people say they felt, and the linear pattern was for picture-plane pairs.
children: The reaction-time pattern is the evidence for rotation.

blocks.text: **Short-term memory** holds about **five to seven items** for roughly **fifteen to twenty seconds** and is easily disrupted by interruption and interference. **Long-term memory** retains large amounts of information for **years or even decades**. They differ in capacity and in duration, so it would be a mistake to treat long-term memory as simply more of short-term memory.
children: Short-term memory is small and brief, and long-term memory is large and lasting.

blocks.text: Rehearsal moves information from short-term toward long-term memory, and retrieval moves it back, so the flow goes both ways and not only toward storage. For instance, you look up a phone number, repeat it to keep it in short-term memory, and later retrieve it from long-term memory back into short-term memory to dial it.
children: Rehearsal moves information toward long-term memory, and retrieval moves it back.

blocks.text: Short-term memory is the active window on the present, and long-term memory is the large body of knowledge stored outside current awareness.
children: One is the current window, and the other is the stored knowledge.

blocks.text: **Declarative memory** is long-term memory for events and knowledge, with two branches: **episodic memory** for events and **semantic memory** for facts. **Procedural memory** is long-term memory for **skills**. Episodic and semantic memory are both inside declarative memory.
children: Declarative covers events and facts, and procedural covers skills.

blocks.text: The memory tree sorts long-term memory by **function** and not by how long things last. Declarative memory is what you can state, and procedural memory is what you can do.
children: Declarative is knowing that, and procedural is knowing how.

blocks.text: For instance, knowing what a bicycle is is declarative, and knowing how to ride one is procedural.
children: The concept is stated, and the skill is performed.

blocks.text: **Encoding** converts information into a form that can be stored, and **storage** keeps it. **Retrieval** is bringing stored information back out when it is needed. A failure to remember could come from a problem at any of the three operations.
children: Memory depends on three operations, and any one can fail.

blocks.text: Forgetting on its own does not show which one failed. For instance, forgetting a familiar name could mean it was never encoded well, was lost from storage, or cannot be retrieved right now. It would be a mistake to name the failed stage from the failure alone.
children: The failure alone does not identify the stage.

blocks.text: Memory is also an active system that can organize and even alter information, so it is not a recording kept unchanged.
children: Memory reconstructs and does not simply replay.

title: Simple vs complex objects in visual short-term memory

blocks.text: **Simple objects**, such as colored squares, need little information to represent, so more of them can be held. **Complex objects**, such as polygons, shaded cubes or Chinese-character-like forms, need more information to represent, so fewer can be held.
children: The more information an object needs, the fewer objects fit.

blocks.text: **Alvarez and Cavanagh (2004)** found that same-different performance depends on how complex the stimuli are. In the change-detection task, colored squares supported a higher estimated capacity than shaded cubes. Capacity is therefore constrained by the amount of information needed to represent the objects.
children: Estimated capacity shrinks as complexity rises.

blocks.text: A capacity for one category of stimulus is not a universal estimate for all visual objects. Do not count every object as an equally sized item.
children: Capacity depends on object complexity and is not one fixed number.
